tips.title: One mole of any gas is 24 dm³
tips.body: At **room temperature and pressure** — AQA defines this as **20 °C and 1 atmosphere** — one mole of *any* gas occupies **24 dm³**. Hydrogen, carbon dioxide, chlorine: the same volume, because volume depends on the number of particles, not on what they are.

tips.title: Volume = moles × 24
tips.body: $$V = n \times 24$$ for a volume in **dm³**, and $n = V \div 24$ to go back. For cm³, use **24000** instead, or convert at the end. Getting a volume from a mass is always two steps: mass → moles → volume.

tips.title: For gases, volumes are in the equation ratio
tips.body: Because equal moles occupy equal volumes, the **volume ratio of gases is the mole ratio**. In $2\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O}$, $100\text{ cm}^3$ of hydrogen needs $50\text{ cm}^3$ of oxygen — no moles needed at all.

tips.title: Only gases count
tips.body: The $24\text{ dm}^3$ rule applies to **gases only**. Solids and liquids in the equation have their own densities and nothing to do with it, so a volume ratio taken straight from the equation is valid only for the substances marked as gases.

tips.title: Conditions change the volume
tips.body: Raise the temperature or lower the pressure and the same amount of gas takes up **more** space. The $24\text{ dm}^3$ figure holds only at room temperature and pressure — which is why the question always states those conditions.

steps.title: Equal moles, equal volumes
steps.body:
*(Higher tier only.)*

Gases behave in a way solids and liquids do not: **equal amounts in moles of any gases occupy the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure**.

The reason is that in a gas the particles are so far apart that their own size hardly matters. What fills the container is mostly empty space, so the volume depends on **how many particles** there are, not on how big or heavy they are.

**The molar volume.** At **room temperature and pressure** — $20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $1$ atmosphere — one mole of any gas occupies $24\text{ dm}^3$.

So one mole of hydrogen ($M_r = 2$, a mass of $2\text{ g}$) and one mole of carbon dioxide ($M_r = 44$, a mass of $44\text{ g}$) both fill $24\text{ dm}^3$ — very different masses, identical volumes.

$$V = n \times 24 \qquad n = \frac{V}{24}$$

with $V$ in dm³. In cm³ the figure is $24000\text{ cm}^3$ per mole.

**Conditions matter.** Warm the gas and it expands; squeeze it and it shrinks. The $24\text{ dm}^3$ value belongs to room temperature and pressure alone, which is why exam questions always say "at room temperature and pressure" before using it.

steps.title: Volumes straight from the equation
steps.body:
When **both** substances are gases, the calculation gets much shorter. Since equal moles occupy equal volumes, the **ratio of volumes is the ratio in the equation** — no conversion to moles is needed at all.

For $$2\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O}$$ the ratio $2 : 1$ means **two volumes** of hydrogen react with **one volume** of oxygen. So $100\text{ cm}^3$ of hydrogen needs $50\text{ cm}^3$ of oxygen — provided both are measured at the same temperature and pressure.

**The units cancel.** Because it is a ratio, the answer comes out in whatever unit you were given: cm³ in, cm³ out. There is no need to convert to dm³ unless the question asks for dm³.

**Only gases.** The shortcut works between gases only. In $\mathrm{CaCO_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_2}$ the carbonate and the oxide are **solids**, so their masses have to go through moles in the ordinary way; only the carbon dioxide uses the molar volume.

**Watch the state symbols.** $\mathrm{H_2O(g)}$ is a gas and counts; $\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$ is a liquid and does not. A question that condenses the water changes the answer, and that is a favourite trap.

steps.title: Working backwards, and in cm³
steps.body:
**From a volume to a mass** the route reverses: divide by $24$ to get moles, apply the equation ratio, then multiply by $M_r$.

$12\text{ dm}^3$ of carbon dioxide at RTP:

- moles $= \dfrac{12}{24} = 0.5\text{ mol}$
- mass $= 0.5 \times 44 = 22\text{ g}$

**Working in cm³.** Laboratory gas volumes are usually measured in cm³ with a gas syringe, so either convert to dm³ first ($\div 1000$) or use $24000\text{ cm}^3$ per mole. Both work; mixing them does not.

$120\text{ cm}^3$ of gas at RTP is $\dfrac{120}{24000} = 0.005\text{ mol}$.

**Limiting reactants apply here too.** If a question gives amounts of two gases, work out which runs out first exactly as before — convert both to moles, divide by the balancing numbers, and take the smaller.

**A sense check worth doing.** A mole of gas is $24\text{ dm}^3$, which is a large box about $29\text{ cm}$ on each side. A laboratory-scale reaction producing a few hundred cm³ therefore involves only a **hundredth** of a mole or so. An answer of hundreds of moles from a test tube is wrong.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. State the volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure, and the conditions AQA means by that.
2. Write the equation linking volume and moles.
3. How many cm³ is $24\text{ dm}^3$?

**Part B.**

4. Find the volume at RTP of $0.5\text{ mol}$ of any gas.
5. Find the volume at RTP of $16\text{ g}$ of oxygen ($M_r = 32$).
6. In $\mathrm{CH_4} + 2\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}$, what volume of oxygen reacts with $25\text{ cm}^3$ of methane?

**Part C.**

7. $10\text{ g}$ of calcium carbonate decomposes fully. Find the volume of carbon dioxide at RTP.
8. A gas syringe collects $96\text{ cm}^3$ of hydrogen. How many moles is that?
9. Explain why one mole of hydrogen and one mole of carbon dioxide occupy the same volume despite their very different masses.

For question 9, the answer is about the number of particles and the space between them.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Use 24, and know the conditions.** AQA specifies $24\text{ dm}^3$ at $20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $1$ atmosphere. The figure $22.4\text{ dm}^3$ belongs to $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and is wrong here; so is quoting $25\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ as room temperature.

**Never convert a mass straight to a volume.** Mass → moles → volume. Multiplying grams by $24$ is a frequent and total loss of the marks.

**Use the volume ratio when both are gases.** It skips two steps and cannot introduce a rounding error. But check the **state symbols** first — water as a liquid does not occupy a gas volume.

**Explain the equal-volume rule properly.** One mole of any gas has the same number of particles, and in a gas the particles are **so far apart that their own size is negligible**, so the volume depends on the count, not on the mass. That is the explanation a mark scheme wants.

**Apply limiting reactants to gases too.** Two gas volumes given means one may run out; divide each by its balancing number just as with masses.

**Keep the unit consistent to the end.** Either work in dm³ throughout, or in cm³ with $24000$. Switching halfway is how factor-of-1000 errors get in.

**Sense-check the size.** A mole of gas fills $24\text{ dm}^3$ — a box about $29\text{ cm}$ across. A gas syringe holding $100\text{ cm}^3$ contains roughly $0.004\text{ mol}$, so a laboratory answer in whole moles is almost certainly wrong.

**Say why conditions are stated.** Gases expand when heated and compress under pressure, so a volume is meaningless unless the conditions are given.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- *(Higher tier, chemistry only.)* **Equal moles of any gases occupy equal volumes** at the same temperature and pressure.
- At **room temperature and pressure** ($20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, $1$ atm), one mole of any gas fills **24 dm³** — or **24000 cm³**.
- $V = n \times 24$ and $n = \dfrac{V}{24}$, with $V$ in dm³.
- **Mass to volume**: mass → moles ($\div M_r$) → volume ($\times 24$).
- **Volume to mass**: volume → moles ($\div 24$) → mass ($\times M_r$).
- Between **gases**, the **volume ratio is the equation ratio** — no moles needed.
- $2\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{O_2}$: $100\text{ cm}^3$ of hydrogen needs $50\text{ cm}^3$ of oxygen.
- Check the **state symbols**: only gases use the molar volume.
- **Limiting reactants** apply to gases as well.
- The rule works because gas particles are **far apart**, so volume depends on the **number** of particles.
- Conditions are always stated, because heating expands a gas and pressure compresses it.

questions.prompt: What is the volume, in dm³, of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure?
What volume, in dm³, does 3 moles of nitrogen occupy at RTP?
One mole of hydrogen and one mole of carbon dioxide are compared at RTP. Which statement is true?
options: They occupy different volumes and have different masses
They occupy the same volume but have different masses
They occupy the same volume and have the same mass
Carbon dioxide occupies more volume because it is heavier
questions.solution: Equal moles occupy **equal volumes**, both 24 dm³ — but hydrogen is 2 g and carbon dioxide 44 g.

What mass, in grams, is 6 dm³ of carbon dioxide at RTP? (Mr of CO₂ = 44)

Why is the temperature and pressure always stated in a gas volume question?

Because a gas expands when heated and compresses under pressure
Because the relative formula mass depends on the conditions

questions.solution: The volume of a fixed amount of gas depends on the conditions: warmer means larger, higher pressure means smaller. The 24 dm³ figure applies only at RTP.

questions.prompt: 10 g of calcium carbonate decomposes fully. What volume of carbon dioxide, in dm³ at RTP, is produced? (Mr of CaCO₃ = 100)
questions.solution: Moles of $\mathrm{CaCO_3} = \dfrac{10}{100} = 0.1$; ratio $1:1$, so $0.1\text{ mol}$ of $\mathrm{CO_2}$; volume $= 0.1 \times 24 = $ **2.4 dm³**.

questions.prompt: Explain why one mole of hydrogen and one mole of carbon dioxide occupy the same volume at the same conditions.
questions.solution: One mole of each contains the **same number of particles**. In a gas the particles are **so far apart that their own size is negligible**, so the volume is set by how many particles there are and the space between them, not by the mass or size of each one.

questions.prompt: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O(g), 100 cm³ of hydrogen reacts completely. What total volume of gas, in cm³, is present after the reaction if all measurements are at the same conditions and the water remains a gas?
questions.solution: The ratio $\mathrm{H_2} : \mathrm{H_2O}$ is $2 : 2$, so $100\text{ cm}^3$ of hydrogen gives **100 cm³** of steam. The oxygen ($50\text{ cm}^3$) is fully used, so the only gas left is the water vapour.

questions.prompt: A student multiplies a mass in grams by 24 to find a gas volume. What is wrong?
options: They should have multiplied by 24000 instead
They should have divided by 24 rather than multiplied
The mass must be converted to moles first, by dividing by the Mr
Nothing, provided the gas is at room temperature and pressure
questions.solution: The molar volume is per **mole**, not per gram. The mass has to be divided by the $M_r$ first; multiplying grams by 24 gives a number with no meaning.

questions.prompt: A gas syringe collects 72 cm³ of hydrogen at RTP from Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. What mass of magnesium, in grams, reacted? (Ar of Mg = 24)
questions.solution: Moles of $\mathrm{H_2} = \dfrac{72}{24000} = 0.003$. The ratio $\mathrm{Mg} : \mathrm{H_2}$ is $1:1$, so $0.003\text{ mol}$ of magnesium. Mass $= 0.003 \times 24 = $ **0.072 g**.

questions.prompt: Why can the volume ratio be taken straight from the equation for gases, but not for solids?
options: Solids do not appear in balanced equations
Gases always react in whole number ratios and solids do not
Equal moles of gases occupy equal volumes, which is not true of solids
The molar volume applies to any substance at room temperature
questions.solution: The shortcut rests on **equal moles occupying equal volumes**, which holds for gases because the particles are far apart. Solids have their own densities, so equal moles of two solids occupy quite different volumes.

markScheme.description: equal moles, equal volumes only for gases

questions.prompt: In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, 40 cm³ of nitrogen is mixed with 90 cm³ of hydrogen. What volume of ammonia, in cm³, forms if the reaction goes to completion?
questions.solution: Divide by the balancing numbers: nitrogen $40 \div 1 = 40$, hydrogen $90 \div 3 = 30$. **Hydrogen is limiting.** The ratio $\mathrm{H_2} : \mathrm{NH_3}$ is $3 : 2$, so $90 \times \frac{2}{3} = $ **60 cm³**.

markScheme.description: divides each volume by its balancing number

questions.prompt: A reaction produces 0.25 dm³ of gas at RTP. How many moles is that, to three decimal places?
questions.solution: $\dfrac{0.25}{24} = 0.0104$, which is **0.010 mol** to three decimal places.

questions.prompt:
A student adds excess hydrochloric acid to 0.12 g of magnesium and collects the hydrogen in a gas syringe: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.

Calculate the volume of hydrogen they should collect at room temperature and pressure, and explain why the volume would be different if the experiment were carried out on a hot day. (Ar of Mg = 24) (6 marks)
questions.solution:
Moles of magnesium $= \dfrac{0.12}{24} = 0.005\text{ mol}$.

The equation shows a $1 : 1$ ratio between magnesium and hydrogen, so $0.005\text{ mol}$ of hydrogen is produced. The acid is in **excess**, so the magnesium is the limiting reactant and all of it reacts.

Volume $= 0.005 \times 24 = \mathbf{0.12\text{ dm}^3}$, which is $\mathbf{120\text{ cm}^3}$ — a sensible reading for a gas syringe.

On a hot day the volume would be **larger**. The molar volume of $24\text{ dm}^3$ applies at room temperature and pressure, $20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $1$ atmosphere. At a higher temperature the gas particles move faster and push further apart, so the **same number of moles** of hydrogen occupies a **greater volume**. The amount of hydrogen produced is unchanged — only the space it fills is different, which is why the conditions must always be stated alongside a gas volume.

markScheme.description: a warmer gas expands, so the volume is larger

examTechnique.body:
One mole of any gas occupies **24 dm³** at room temperature and pressure — AQA's $20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $1$ atmosphere. Use $V = n \times 24$, or $24000$ if you are working in cm³.

A mass never becomes a volume directly: go **mass → moles → volume**. Between two **gases**, take the volume ratio straight from the equation — but check the state symbols first, because only gases count.
examinerErrors: Quoting room temperature as 25 degrees C.
Multiplying a mass in grams by 24.
Mixing cm3 and dm3 in the same calculation.
Applying the volume ratio to a solid or a liquid.
Ignoring a limiting reactant when two gas volumes are given.
Explaining equal volumes by saying gases are light.
Giving an answer in moles that is impossible for laboratory apparatus.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer uses 24 dm³ with the right conditions, routes every mass through moles, and takes the volume ratio directly from the equation when — and only when — both substances are gases, checking the state symbols to be sure. It handles cm³ consistently, applies limiting reactants to gas volumes as readily as to masses, and explains the equal-volume rule by the number of particles and the spacing between them. It sense-checks the size of its answer against the apparatus, and can say why the conditions have to be stated at all.
